header:
Date: 2025-06-18
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes
Attendees: Olivia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Zenith ML), Luca Marino (Zenith Infra), Sam Torres (Zenith CTO)
summary: SE-led deep dive on KV cache behavior under long-context workloads. Discussed spill-to-disk/paging thresholds, prefetch heuristics, prefix reuse sensitivity, and how batching/quantization interact with cache pressure. Action items: collect KV eviction telemetry, run soak benchmark with spill enabled, share prefetch config recommendations.
topics: Long-context workload patterns and batching interactions
Quantization impact on memory footprint and cache pressure
VPC/on-prem constraints for spill storage and IOPS
Telemetry and diagnostics: eviction logs, latency histograms, KV hit-rate by prefix
transcript:
[00:00] Olivia Chen (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll run about 50 minutes, Marcus is going to take us through the KV cache troubleshooting and some config knobs we recommend for long-context scoring workloads.

[00:18] Marcus Patel (SE): Hey, hi all. quick agenda: first we look at what you've seen — Luca, can you give a 2 min on your symptoms? Then we'll map to the runtime behaviors and propose immediate mitigations.

[00:29] Luca Marino (Infra): Yeah, thanks. So over the last two weeks we've seen tail latency spikes when sequences go beyond 12k tokens. It looks like throughput is fine on smaller contexts but once a few requests with long prefixes hit the system we see evictions and then a partial stall while the runtime pages KV back in. The node-level mem goes high and then there's a lot of I/O.

[00:50] Priya Nair (ML): Also noticed quality regressions when the prefix reuse is high across concurrent users — sometimes the same prefix is reused by many sessions and then later the cache seems to thrash.

[01:05] Marcus: Right, that matches what we expect when the working set outgrows the in-memory KV. A couple of terms: 'spill-to-disk' we use for paging the KV entries to local fast SSD, separate from swapping the whole process. We also have prefetch heuristics that can warm likely-needed KV segments.

[01:22] Sam Torres (CTO): Quick question — are we talking about OS swap or Redwood-managed spill? We can't allow kernel swap in our on-prem nodes.

[01:29] Marcus: Good callout. Redwood's runtime avoids OS swap by reserving memory and managing KV spill within the process. On your private/on-prem setup we recommend provisioning local NVMe for spill with guaranteed IOPS; otherwise you'll see the exact swap-like stalls you described.

[01:47] Olivia: I'll add that to the config doc — we have a recommended spec for private deployments that lists NVMe capacity and io1/io2 or equivalent IOPS.

[02:00] Luca: We're on VMs with network-attached storage, not local NVMe, which is part of the problem. We can request local disks but it's a change to infra.

[02:10] Marcus: Ok, two immediate levers: 1) increase in-memory KV capacity (bigger instance) 2) enable spill-to-disk to a local fast mount to avoid OS swap. If local NVMe isn't available, a temporary mitigation is to tighten max-seq / reject or route long-context requests to a dedicated pool.

[02:33] Priya: We're trying to avoid rejecting user requests. What's the perf delta with spill-to-disk enabled?

[02:38] Marcus: Good question. With local NVMe and optimized IO path we typically see an extra ~20-60ms per token when a cold page is pulled versus in-memory hit. But that varies — on slow network storage it can jump to multiple seconds for the first tokens while pages stream in.

[02:56] Sam: That matches our ops dashboards — occasional multi-second tails.

[03:03] Marcus: So prefetching becomes important. Our prefetch heuristics look at access patterns: recent prefix frequency, request concurrency, and estimated next-token span. If a prefix has been used N times in the last T seconds we proactively fetch its segments.

[03:22] Priya: How do you avoid prefetching everything and increasing pressure?

[03:26] Marcus: We use a score combining recency and reuse with a budget per worker. There's a hard cap to prevent runaway prefetch. Also we prefer segment-level prefetch — small units — and prefer coalescing adjacent segments when access locality is high.

[03:40] Luca: You mentioned 'segments' — are those KV shards aligned to layers, or token-range based?

[03:46] Marcus: Segment is an internal contiguous KV slice, typically aligned to KV indexes for attention caches. Not exactly layer — more like kv-offset ranges that the runtime can map quickly.

[03:55] Olivia: We're going to share a diagram after this — shows segments, segment indexes, and spill files.

[04:02] Priya: Can prefetch cause correctness regressions? Like if it pulls a stale segment for a model updated in place?

[04:10] Marcus: No, cache entries are versioned with model and rollout IDs. When you pin a model version we avoid accidental stale pages. But if you do a live rollout and change the model id without invalidating caches you'll definitely see mismatches — we recommend the runtime invalidate affected segments on model swap.

[04:28] Sam: What's the eviction policy? LRU? LFU? Or something bespoke?

[04:32] Marcus: It's a cost-aware LRU with weights. We compute an approximate recency score and a decay based on segment size and access cost. We also prioritize keeping KV for recent active sessions—think a sliding window of hot prefixes.

[04:46] Priya: We've got a lot of shared prefixes from templated conversation starters, which I think is causing reuse spikes. Any quick wins there?

[04:53] Marcus: Yes — prefix hashing and deduping can really help. You can normalize certain template parts so the runtime can reuse one canonical prefix instead of a million minor variants. We'll share a normalization recipe.

[05:05] Olivia: Note: normalization may change semantics; do that only for high-variance low-impact prefixes.

[05:12] Luca: On the infra side, we saw that when multiple workers attempt to fetch the same segment there's a thundering herd. Any mitigation?

[05:19] Marcus: We have a singleflight mechanism: first fetcher becomes owner; others wait on an in-process promise. Also we apply jittered backoff for retries. But if your worker count is very high you still need a global prefetch coordinator or route similar prefixes to the same worker pool.

[05:37] Priya: Does batching interact badly with KV pressure? We batch requests to maximize throughput.

[05:41] Marcus: Batching increases the effective working set because different requests' KV ranges merge. For long-context, a batch of 16 with partially overlapping prefixes can blow past memory. Strategies: smaller max-batch for long-context pool, dynamic batch sizing based on ave prefix-length, or per-request hint to the runtime that this is low-latency single-request path.

[06:02] Sam: What about quantization — does that actually reduce KV size?

[06:06] Marcus: Yes, lower-precision KV entries reduce memory. Quantization of KV (e.g., 8-bit) halves or quarters footprints depending on scheme. But be careful: quantization noise can introduce subtle quality diffs for exact-match long-context tasks. For most generation tasks it's fine, for retrieval-augmented or scoring you might want higher precision.

[06:26] Priya: So a hybrid — keep KV in 16-bit for scoring, 8-bit for generation? Is that supported?

[06:32] Marcus: We support per-model or per-layer quant profiles. The runtime can coerce precision per segment; it's a bit advanced but we can recommend conservative profiles for your scoring workloads.

[06:44] Luca: Back to the paging — what metrics should we ship you to diagnose better?

[06:49] Marcus: Three things first: 1) eviction log with timestamps and segment IDs 2) latency histogram at token level including cold-page penalty buckets 3) KV hit-rate broken down by prefix hash and session id. If you can provide a sample of the long-context requests that trigger evictions, that's gold.

[07:06] Priya: We'll get that. One more — can we tune the spill threshold dynamically? Like reduce in-memory reserves during low traffic?

[07:13] Marcus: Yes, our runtime supports adaptive thresholds: it lowers reserved memory when CPU load is low and increases when you have more hot sessions. We also have a 'grace' period so it doesn't oscillate on short bursts.

[07:27] Olivia: Marcus, can you walk through a hypothetical sequence with numbers? Say 256GB node, model X uses 120GB KV for active set, what happens when a 20-concurrent long-request flood arrives?

[07:39] Marcus: Sure. If active set + incoming demand > reserved (say reserved=180GB) then eviction begins. The runtime picks cold segments by recency weight; if spill-to-disk is enabled it asynchronously writes them to local NVMe and frees RAM, then incoming requests reading those segments trigger reads. If NVMe read latency is 200us you're fine. If it's multi-ms you'll get tail latency. If no local NVMe and you rely on network storage you get large tail. So for 20 concurrent heavy requests you'll want either: increase reserved memory, or route them to a dedicated pool with spill capacity, or enable aggressive prefetch before the flood based on traffic surge detection.

[08:20] Luca: And if we can't add local NVMe quickly, is routing to dedicated pool the least invasive?

[08:24] Marcus: Yes, isolate long-context to smaller worker pools with tuned batch sizes and higher memory. It's a quick config change.

[08:33] Priya: How about the diagnostics UI? We're seeing aggregate numbers in console but need per-prefix heatmap.

[08:39] Marcus: We have a per-prefix heatmap in Redwood Console experiments tab — not enabled by default for privacy reasons. We can enable for your account if you sign the telemetry toggle. It will show prefix frequency, hit-rate, eviction count.

[08:54] Priya: We'll sign the toggle.

[08:58] Olivia: We should also talk about retention — how long do spill files live?

[09:02] Marcus: Spill files are ephemeral by default and follow process lifecycle. You can configure retention for debug periods. For Private installs you can also route spill to an encrypted mount. We integrate with KMS so metadata and keys are managed.

[09:14] Sam: KMS integration is mandatory for us. We need to ensure keys never leave our HSM.

[09:19] Marcus: On private we support customer-managed KMS/HSM. We'll include the HSM integration notes in the security annex.

[09:28] Priya: On the prefetch heuristics, can we provide hints client-side? Like suggest which prefixes will be used next?

[09:34] Marcus: Yes, you can include a 'prefetch_hint' header or metadata in the request. The runtime will respect it but still apply budget and dedupe. It's useful if you can predict continuation (e.g., predictable multi-step agent).

[09:48] Luca: We'll prototype sending hints from our orchestration layer.

[09:52] Marcus: Another strategy: prefix canonicalization at the application level — fewer unique prefixes means better reuse.

[09:58] Priya: About the thundering herd — you said singleflight helps. Do you have metrics on how often that reduces duplicate fetches?

[10:05] Marcus: In our benchmarks, singleflight reduces duplicate fetches by ~70% under moderate concurrency. Under extreme concurrency you still need routing or sticky session to keep it at bay.

[10:15] Sam: We run a multi-tenant cluster. Would it make sense to pin certain high-value tenants to dedicated pools?

[10:20] Marcus: Absolutely — tenant isolation is a common pattern. You can pin heavy users to dedicated nodes with larger reserved memory and local NVMe to guarantee SLAs.

[10:30] Olivia: Quick pause — any other infra constraints we should call out?

[10:35] Luca: Network latency between nodes and storage is the main one. Also our cloud provider charges heavy for local NVMe, but it may be worth it.

[10:43] Marcus: Cost vs latency tradeoff — another lever is model quantization or using a smaller KV-friendly model variant for long-context tails. You can fallback to a slim model with lower KV footprint when pressure is high.

[10:55] Priya: Does Redwood support automatic model fallback?

[10:58] Marcus: Yes, routing policies can fallback to a compatible variant. It does require some validation. We'll talk through rollback/quality thresholds in the follow-up.

[11:08] Olivia: We're approaching the middle — Marcus, can you share the rough timeline for the recommended changes?

[11:14] Marcus: Sure: immediate (days): enable telemetry toggle, export eviction logs, route long-context to dedicated pool. Short-term (1–2 weeks): enable spill-to-disk to local NVMe, enable prefetch with conservative budget. Medium (3–4 weeks): run extended soak, tune quant profiles, implement normalization of prefixes.

[11:33] Priya: Sounds good. Can you email the config snippets?

[11:36] Olivia: Yes, I'll send the snippets and the prefetch heuristics doc.

[11:40] Marcus: One more advanced note — segment coalescing can reduce IO overhead by merging adjacent cold pages when we detect sequential access. It's beneficial for streaming-style long visits. But it increases write amplification during eviction, so use carefully.

[11:55] Luca: That may be fine if we have good NVMe endurance. We'll check.

[12:00] Priya: For the soak benchmark, what workload shape would you recommend?

[12:04] Marcus: Mix: 80% small contexts (<=2k), 20% long contexts (8–16k) with varying overlap across sessions; concurrency up to your production peak. Important to include the 'hot prefix storms' pattern — e.g., 5 sudden requests reusing same prefix.

[12:21] Sam: We'll prepare synthetic traffic and run with profiling enabled.

[12:25] Marcus: Great. Also enable the debug kv_trace at low sampling (1%) to avoid perf impact; it'll show per-segment read/write timing.

[12:36] Priya: Does debug kv_trace capture user content? We need PII considerations.

[12:40] Marcus: It captures segment IDs and timing, not raw prompt text unless you enable the detailed trace; by default it's metadata only. We'll provide a privacy breakdown.

[12:52] Olivia: Ok — any other questions from Zenith team?

[12:57] Priya: One quick architecture question: for private deployments, can spill files be mounted on a remote iSCSI volume with guaranteed IOPS?

[13:04] Marcus: Technically yes, but local NVMe is strongly recommended. Remote iSCSI with guaranteed IOPS is acceptable if latency is sub-ms. If it's multi-ms, you'll see tail spikes.

[13:18] Luca: We'll check our storage options.

[13:22] Olivia: We're about 40 minutes in — quick recap before we close.

[13:27] Marcus: Recap: root cause likely working set > in-memory reserved KV, causing evictions and readbacks that look like paging. Immediate mitigations: route long-context to dedicated pool, enable spill-to-disk to local NVMe, enable conservative prefetch, send eviction logs and sample traces. Longer term: quant profiles, prefix normalization, segment coalescing tuning.

[13:49] Priya: And action items?

[13:52] Olivia: I'll put those in the notes: Marcus exports eviction telemetry; Priya sends long-context prompt set; Olivia sends prefetch config and snippets; schedule follow-up soak next week.

[14:05] Sam: If we get this right it should eliminate the multi-second tails. Appreciate the partnership.

[14:11] Marcus: Totally. We'll also include a recommended alert: percent of tokens served with cold-page penalty > X% triggers autoscale or routing changes.

[14:23] Priya: Good idea.

[14:26] Olivia: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the deck and the console link.

[14:31] Luca: Thanks all.

[14:34] [END OF ZOOM TRANSCRIPT]
